subject: geography
title: US Middle School Geography — Urbanization and Cities
subtitle: How cities grow, change land use, create opportunities, and face sustainability challenges.
description: This pack helps students revise how and why cities grow, including migration, land use, transportation, urban challenges, and sustainable planning. It uses urban vocabulary, map and data skills, and case studies such as New York City, Phoenix, Lagos, Curitiba, and Tokyo.

data.targetWord: the growth of cities and the increasing share of people living in urban areas

examples.en-US: Urbanization changes where people live, work, travel, and use resources.

data.targetWord: a town or city where many people, buildings, and services are close together

examples.en-US: New York City is an urban area with dense housing, jobs, and services.

data.targetWord: countryside or small settlements with fewer people and more open land

examples.en-US: A rural area may include farms, ranches, villages, and forests.

data.targetWord: a mostly residential area on the edge of a city

examples.en-US: A suburb may have houses, schools, shopping centers, and commuters.

data.targetWord: a large city together with nearby suburbs and connected towns

examples.en-US: Greater Boston is a metropolitan area because it includes the central city and surrounding communities.

data.targetWord: the number of people living in a place

examples.en-US: A city with a population of 650,000 needs enough housing and services for those residents.

data.targetWord: the number of people living in a given area

examples.en-US: Population density is often measured as people per square mile.

data.targetWord: the movement of people from one place to another

examples.en-US: Migration from rural areas to cities can increase urban population.

data.targetWord: a reason that encourages people to leave a place

examples.en-US: Drought, conflict, and lack of jobs can be push factors.

data.targetWord: a reason that attracts people to a place

examples.en-US: Jobs, schools, hospitals, and safety can be pull factors.

data.targetWord: an area with shared features

examples.en-US: The Sun Belt is a region of the United States with warm climates and fast-growing cities.

data.targetWord: the natural and human surroundings of a place

examples.en-US: A city environment includes rivers, roads, buildings, parks, weather, and people.

data.targetWord: the usual weather patterns of a place over a long time

examples.en-US: Phoenix has a hot desert climate that affects water use and cooling needs.

data.targetWord: the short-term condition of the atmosphere

examples.en-US: Rain today is weather, not climate.

data.targetWord: something people use from the environment

examples.en-US: Fresh water, land, energy, and minerals are resources that cities need.

data.targetWord: the basic systems that help a place function

examples.en-US: Roads, bridges, water pipes, power lines, and rail lines are infrastructure.

data.targetWord: the way people use land in a place

examples.en-US: Housing, stores, factories, parks, roads, and airports are different land uses.

data.targetWord: the main commercial center of a city

examples.en-US: A downtown CBD usually has offices, stores, banks, and services.

data.targetWord: housing built without official planning or legal permission

examples.en-US: Informal settlements may grow when cities lack enough affordable planned housing.

data.targetWord: neighborhood change caused by investment that often raises costs and may displace residents

examples.en-US: Gentrification can turn older housing into expensive apartments.

data.targetWord: spread-out city growth into surrounding land

examples.en-US: Urban sprawl can convert farmland into housing, roads, and shopping centers.

data.targetWord: meeting today’s needs without harming the ability of future generations to meet theirs

examples.en-US: A sustainable city protects people, the economy, and the environment over time.

data.targetWord: shared transport systems used by many people

examples.en-US: Buses, subways, commuter rail, and light rail are public transportation.

data.targetWord: the pattern where cities are hotter than nearby rural areas

examples.en-US: Concrete, asphalt, and rooftops help create the urban heat island effect.

data.targetWord: parks, gardens, trees, and natural areas in a city

examples.en-US: Green space can provide shade, recreation, cleaner air, and stormwater absorption.

data.targetWord: a city with more than 10 million people

examples.en-US: Tokyo, Delhi, and Shanghai are examples of megacities.

data.targetWord: a city with major global influence

examples.en-US: London, New York, and Tokyo are world cities because they shape global finance, culture, and transport.

data.targetWord: the actual physical land where a city is built

examples.en-US: A river, harbor, flat land, hills, soil, climate, and natural resources are site features.

data.targetWord: how a city is connected to other places

examples.en-US: Roads, rail lines, airports, trade routes, and nearby cities describe situation.

data.targetWord: land mainly used for homes

examples.en-US: Apartments, houses, and condos are residential land uses.

data.targetWord: land mainly used for shops, offices, banks, and restaurants

examples.en-US: A downtown shopping street is commercial land use.

data.targetWord: land mainly used for factories, warehouses, and shipping

examples.en-US: Industrial areas are often near rail lines, highways, or ports.

data.targetWord: water that flows over land after rain instead of soaking into the ground

examples.en-US: Concrete and asphalt can increase runoff in cities.

data.targetWord: planning that connects housing, jobs, schools, stores, and transportation while limiting wasteful sprawl

examples.en-US: Smart growth can include mixed-use neighborhoods and public transit.

data.targetWord: development that combines homes, shops, offices, and public spaces in the same area

examples.en-US: Mixed-use development can reduce travel distances and make neighborhoods more active.

data.targetWord: fair protection from environmental harm and fair access to environmental benefits for all communities

examples.en-US: Environmental justice can mean adding trees, transit, and pollution controls in underserved neighborhoods.

data.targetWord: a pattern where people need cars for most daily trips

examples.en-US: Spread-out suburbs often have more car dependence than dense city centers.

data.targetWord: housing that people can pay for without losing access to other basic needs

examples.en-US: Affordable housing matters because fast-growing cities can become too expensive for many residents.

data.targetWord: unequal access to housing, parks, schools, transit, clean air, and political voice within a city

examples.en-US: Urban inequality can mean one neighborhood has many trees while another has more heat and pollution.

data.targetWord: the chance that water will cover land where people live, travel, or work

examples.en-US: Cities near rivers, coasts, or low-lying land must plan for flood risk.

data.targetWord: a route where public transportation and higher-density development are planned together

examples.en-US: Curitiba used transit corridors to connect bus rapid transit with city growth.

data.targetWord: a bus system designed to move people quickly using features such as dedicated routes or priority service

examples.en-US: Curitiba is often studied for bus rapid transit planning.

data.targetWord: new building on land that was previously open, rural, or undeveloped

examples.en-US: New housing spreading into farmland north of a city is greenfield development.

data.targetWord: how suitable a place is for healthy, safe, fair, and enjoyable daily life

examples.en-US: Transit, housing, parks, schools, safety, and clean air all affect livability.

data.sentence: The growth of cities and the increasing share of people living in urban areas is called ____.
data.hint: Starts with u

data.sentence: The number of people living in a certain area is population ____.
data.hint: People per square mile is one example.

data.sentence: A reason people leave a place is a ____ factor.
data.hint: It pushes people away.

data.sentence: A reason people are attracted to a place is a ____ factor.
data.hint: It pulls people toward a place.

data.sentence: The long-term usual weather pattern of a place is its ____.
data.hint: Not the same as today’s weather.

data.sentence: A city and its surrounding suburbs and connected towns form a ____ area.
data.hint: Greater Boston is one example.

data.sentence: Roads, bridges, water pipes, and power lines are examples of ____.
data.hint: Basic systems that help a place function.

data.sentence: Spread-out city growth into surrounding land is called urban ____.
data.hint: It often converts farmland or habitat.

data.sentence: The main commercial center of a city is the central business ____.
data.hint: Often called downtown.

data.sentence: Cities are often warmer than nearby rural areas because asphalt and concrete absorb ____.
data.hint: This creates an urban heat island.

data.sentence: Parks, gardens, trees, and natural areas in a city are examples of green ____.
data.hint: They can cool neighborhoods and support recreation.

data.sentence: A city with more than 10 million people is called a ____.
data.hint: Tokyo is one example.

data.sentence: A city’s physical land features, such as rivers, harbors, and flat land, describe its ____.
data.hint: This means the actual land where it is built.

data.sentence: A city’s links to roads, rail lines, airports, markets, and other cities describe its ____.
data.hint: This focuses on connections.

data.sentence: Land mainly used for homes is ____ land use.
data.hint: Apartments and houses fit this type.

data.sentence: Land mainly used for shops, offices, banks, and restaurants is ____ land use.
data.hint: Downtown stores fit this type.

data.sentence: Land mainly used for factories, warehouses, and shipping is ____ land use.
data.hint: It is often near highways, rail lines, or ports.

data.sentence: Cities often need flood planning because hard surfaces increase rainwater ____.
data.hint: Water flows over the surface instead of soaking in.

data.sentence: Planning that connects homes, jobs, schools, stores, and transit is often called smart ____.
data.hint: It tries to reduce wasteful sprawl.

data.sentence: Fair protection from environmental harm and fair access to benefits is environmental ____.
data.hint: It matters when some neighborhoods face more pollution or heat.

data.title: How Urban Sprawl Can Happen
data.instruction: Put the stages of urban sprawl in a logical order.
items: City population grows.
Demand for housing increases.
Homes are built farther from the city center.
More roads, parking lots, and shopping centers are built.
Longer car trips and more traffic become common.
Farmland or habitat is converted to urban land.

data.title: Rural-to-Urban Migration Decision
data.instruction: Put the steps of a common migration pattern in order.
items: A rural household faces a pressure such as low farm income, drought, or limited services.
Family members compare conditions in rural and urban places.
City pull factors such as jobs, schools, hospitals, or relatives become important.
One or more people move to the city.
The city population grows and demand for housing and services rises.

data.title: Using Urban Data Carefully
data.instruction: Put the data-use steps in a strong geographic order.
items: Identify what the map, graph, or table measures.
Check the place, time period, and source of the data.
Describe the pattern shown by the data.
Ask what the data does not show or might hide.
Use evidence and local context before making a planning decision.

data.title: Planning a More Sustainable Neighborhood
data.instruction: Put the planning choices in a logical design order.
items: Identify the community’s needs, such as housing, school access, transit, heat, and stormwater.
Choose land uses that place homes, services, and green space close together.
Plan safe sidewalks, bike routes, and public transportation connections.
Add trees, parks, shade, and stormwater features.
Check whether the plan is fair, affordable, and useful for different residents.
